bearings.paper_claim: Table 2 daily-close campaign regressions give S&P coefficients 0.087 (daily), 0.128 (5-day) and 0.243 (20-day); oil -7.269 (5-day) and -12.570 (20-day). Text says the Table 2 equity effect is roughly a factor of ten larger than Table 1 (0.016 at 10-min differences, n=104). Authors attribute the gap to bias from reverse causation and common shocks. The OLS upper-bound statement (p.11, fn 14) concerns the reverse regression of the Bush probability on the S&P (2.3 and 3.3 pp per 10 percent rise), and holds if the shock correlation is non-negative, a sufficient condition.
bearings.paper_location: Table 1 p.7; Table 2 p.10; text p.10-11 and fn 14 p.11
bearings.system_side: SEATS-W regresses the week's Democratic share of giving on the prior week's change in 538 expected Democratic seats, pairing each week with the latest forecast available strictly before the week starts. 2022 House, 17 weeks, -3.47 pp per seat, EXPLORATORY. The code header presents it as a correlation and does not address common shocks.
bearings.code_ref: C:/Users/pgoff/Mentat/sector_growth_study/code/R/sgs_seats.R:15-21 (design and as-of pairing); sgs_seats.R:52-54 (SEATS-W gate); sgs_seats.R:66-75 (inference notes)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The size of the bias does not transfer to PAC giving (lumpy, deadline-driven, different series), but the existence of a common-shock confound does: the as-of lag removes within-week ordering, not shared news moving forecasts and giving together. The negative slope cannot be read as donors moving toward or away from the expected winner. An upper-bound argument needs a stated correlation sign, which SEATS-W does not supply.
bearings.verifier_note: Numbers, the factor-of-ten statement and the reverse-causation attribution check out against the text (Table 2 p.10, p.10-11). The OLS upper-bound sentence was attached to the Table 2 regression and stated as only-if; corrected in paper_claim. The 55 to 30 to 95 percent exit-poll path is in the text at p.5-6 and p.9.

bearings.paper_claim: Identification uses two discrete election-night jumps in the Bush probability: the 2004 exit-poll leak (about 55 to 30 percent, then 95) and the 2000 Florida calls. Equity effects are 10- and 30-minute regressions (Table 1); a Wald estimator is stated explicitly only for yields (TIP and IEF, p.8-9). Footnote 9 splits the sample at 8pm and 10pm to test feedback. The paper does not recommend event-window designs; footnote 13 names instrumental variables as the ideal and leaves it open.
bearings.paper_location: p.4-9; Figures 1-3; Table 1 p.7; fn 9 p.6; fn 13 p.12
bearings.system_side: SEATS-W uses every pre-election week as an observation, with a residual block bootstrap conditional on the forecast path. No event-window design around large forecast moves exists in sgs_seats.R.
bearings.code_ref: C:/Users/pgoff/Mentat/sector_growth_study/code/R/sgs_seats.R:66-75 (bootstrap and inference notes); sgs_seats.R:93-94 (dated 2022 forecast histories in hand)
bearings.transfer_conditions: An event-window design needs forecast jumps from news plausibly unrelated to donor behaviour, and transaction-dated giving fine enough around each jump. The 2022 538 run timestamps could support a search, which stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062) and names its window and denominator. A Wald ratio needs a donor-side response series that the paper does not have.
bearings.verifier_note: The exit-poll path and the fn 9 split are verified. The event-window recommendation is the analyst's inference, not the paper's; the Wald ratio is explicit only for yields. Rewritten to what the paper says.

bearings.paper_claim: Partisan shock is the indicator of a Republican president minus the pre-election prediction-market probability of a Republican president. Table 3, 1880-2004: coefficient 0.0255 (SE 0.0082) without the incumbent term and 0.0248 (SE 0.0084) with it; incumbent-party term -0.0046 (SE 0.0084). Congressional control could not be tested because markets did not track it before 1994 (fn 19).
bearings.paper_location: Historical evidence section p.15-17; Table 3 p.17; fn 19 p.17
bearings.system_side: SHIFT in sgs_panel.R builds exp_shift as expected Democratic control minus current Democratic control, the Democratic-sign version. The brain study contract defines Shift as P minus RMajNow with P the Republican majority probability. Preview: chamber-stacked -0.04, p 0.76 (2021-25).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Shift is an expected change in control before the election. The paper's shock is realized outcome minus prior expectation, so it transfers only to post-election giving. Independent shocks equal the number of elections, so any estimate is few-cluster and must say so. The sign convention must be stated as Democratic control, not Republican P.
bearings.verifier_note: Coefficients, SEs and the shock definition reproduce from the paper, although Table 3 column alignment is garbled in extraction. The rel's description of the code as Shift = P minus RMajNow with P Republican is a sign-convention mismatch: code uses Democratic expected minus current.

related.why: Furnas et al. estimate revenue effects for party-tied lobbying firms after House-control flips, a control-shock design close to the SEATS and SHIFT question; the outcome is firm revenue, not donations.
Imai and Kim show that two-way fixed-effects estimates rely on linearity for a causal reading, which bounds what the SHIFT and SEATS-W panel regressions can claim.
